  • The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue held its first leaders’ meeting in more than two years on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

Recent findings suggest that the highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan challenges a plea for medical treatment.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: High-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen captures the attention of Indian policymakers, Bangladesh is cleared to receive U.S. International Development Finance Corp. funding, and jailed former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan complications a plea for medical treatment.

Recent findings suggest that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue held its first leaders’ meeting in more than two years on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in Manila, Philippines, on Tuesday. Australia, India, Japan, and the United States announced initiatives including cybersecurity collaboration, a cable connectivity framework, and a maritime surveillance exercise.

Industry observers note that the Quad meeting likely brought some relief for Newly introduced Delhi. The grouping is crucial for India’s foreign-policy interests, bringing together some of its closest security partners in an effort to counter China. (However, the Quad states rarely mention Beijing in their public messaging about the grouping to avoid antagonizing the superpower.).

Though India has engineered a rapprochement with China in the last two years, taking steps to reduce border tensions and scale up trade and investment, they remain bitter strategic rivals. India prioritizes opportunities to work multilaterally to push back against China’s power through non-security collaborations in areas such as technology and infrastructure investment.

Scheduling issues and U.S.-India tensions have prevented high-level Quad engagement since September 2024. Quad supporters will point to Tuesday’s meeting as an indication of the grouping’s resilience, much like how it bounced back from quiescence in 2017—interestingly, with another summit in Manila when each member’s ties with China faced increasing strain.

Recent findings suggest that still, the Quad remains mired in uncertainty, mainly because of U.S. President Donald Trump. His administration’s signaling about taking a softer approach to competition with China, coupled with silence about the fate of the U.S. Indo-Pacific strategy, suggests that the current White House may not be prepared to throw its full support behind the Quad.

Though an incoming Democratic Congress might take a tougher line on China, this is unlikely to shape the Trump administration’s thinking on the Quad. As a result, the wider ASEAN summit arguably held more immediate significance for New Delhi than the Quad meeting.

Industry observers note that indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has long sought to step up India’s game in Southeast Asia—a region home to key Indian partners and multiple growing economies. India has especially strong incentives to ramp up engagement given China’s large footprint there. In that sense, the stakes were high for Modi’s engagement with ASEAN leaders this week.

Upcoming Delhi will now closely watch as Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin hold a historic trilateral meeting on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. There is a lack of clarity, but the discussion will reportedly include the Iran war and nuclear nonproliferation.

Industry observers note that such themes are unlikely to concern India, which has a strong interest in the wars in both Iran and Ukraine coming to an end. But the summit will be a vindication of sorts for Fresh Delhi. In 2025, Trump slammed a meeting among Modi, Xi, and Putin in China; now, he is coming to the same table.

It has been revealed that however, the boost that China is likely to get from the trilateral isn’t ideal for India. The U.S., Chinese, and Russian leaders have never had such a formal face-to-face exchange. Beijing’s capacity to convene the three leaders, against a backdrop of long-standing U.S.-Russia hostility, is a major diplomatic achievement.

Recent findings suggest that for New Delhi, the biggest takeaway from this week’s high-level diplomacy in Manila and Shenzhen is that the Quad leaders’ meeting was a relative sideshow. The ASEAN and APEC summits will generate more attention and hold more immediate significance for Indian policymakers.

According to recent reports, bangladesh cleared for DFC investment. The U.S. International Development Finance Corp. (DFC) announced on Monday that Bangladesh was now eligible to receive its financing. The DFC, which mobilizes private investment, has taken on added importance since the demise of the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) last year.

Until now, Bangladesh was ineligible for DFC financing because of U.S. concerns about labor conditions in the country. Negotiations between Washington and Dhaka to address these concerns and clear the way go back to the Biden administration.

The announcement couldn’t come at a better time for Bangladesh, which faces serious development challenges and severe economic stress. Some of its most pressing challenges—such as fuel shortages and the world’s worst measles epidemic—are tied to energy and healthcare, two of DFC’s priority areas for investment.

DFC-funded projects could bring a boost to U.S.-Bangladesh relations. Development cooperation, for years embodied by the large USAID mission in Dhaka, has long been a major component of the relationship.

Khan concerns plea for medical treatment. Lawyers for Imran Khan sent an open letter on Monday from the jailed former prime minister to top judges in Pakistan, imploring them to secure better healthcare for Khan and his wife, who is also in prison. In the letter, Khan says he is suffering from high blood pressure and is at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest.

For months, Khan’s lawyers, family, and supporters have mentioned his health is worsening, while officials say he is stable and regularly monitored by prison doctors. In August, Pakistan’s Supreme Court ordered Khan to be transferred to a private hospital for an extended period; he was instead brought to a government hospital and only briefly.

Industry observers note that concern for Khan’s health was one reason why leaders of the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party announced nationwide protests last month. But aside from some demonstrations in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, the only one governed by the PTI, the campaign didn’t materialize. The party might be back-channeling with the country’s leadership to secure concessions for Khan.

British royals visit India. The United Kingdom’s Prince William and Princess Catherine completed a three-day visit to India on Wednesday. They began their trip in Mumbai, where they participated in the Earthshot Prize ceremony. William founded the award, which focuses on developing new solutions to climate change.

According to recent reports, the royal couple then traveled to Newly introduced Delhi, where they met Modi. Their visit underscores the strong ties between India and its former colonizer. U.K.-India relations have deepened in recent years, buoyed most recently by a free trade deal that formally entered into force in July.

For that matter, U.K.-Pakistan ties are also quite warm; William and Kate made a visit there in 2019. Deep people-to-people ties, thanks in part to large Indian and Pakistani diasporas in the U.K., help bolster these relationships. British colonial rule may have left a problematic legacy in the subcontinent, but diplomacy today is in a good place.

Recent findings suggest that new Delhi hosts an arts and culture forum this weekend under the banner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). The idea for the Civilisational Dialogue Forum came from India, which will head the event even though Pakistan is the current SCO chair. Pakistan’s climate change minister, Musadik Malik, will travel to New Delhi to represent Islamabad.

With India-Pakistan ties so tense in recent years, the rare occasions when senior ministers from one country have traveled to the other have mostly come in their capacity as SCO members.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari traveled to India for an SCO summit in 2023, while Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar went to Pakistan the next year. Malik’s visit, however, comes at an especially fraught moment, with the relationship essentially frozen since the brief military conflict between India and Pakistan in 2025.

Looking ahead, a big question is whether Modi will travel to Pakistan for the SCO leaders’ summit scheduled for next August. Modi visited Pakistan in December 2015, early in his first term. Several days after his trip, Pakistani terrorists attacked an Indian Air Force base. Since that incident, Modi’s government has taken an especially hard line toward Pakistan.

Even though Jaishankar went to Pakistan in 2024, it is unlikely that Modi himself will make the trip next year—especially if the protest movement against his government that has gripped India in recent months remains active.

In a recent development, in the Daily Mirror, writer K.K.S. Perera analyzes Sri Lanka’s fresh budget: “Has the 2027 Budget adequately addressed the economic difficulties confronting ordinary Sri Lankans? The answer must be examined against people’s actual living conditions rather than the Government’s financial projections, development promises, and announcements.”.

It has been revealed that in the Print, education expert Archana Dalmia reflects on Italian-born Indian politician Sonia Gandhi’s upcoming memoir, Belonging. “Destiny had written a very different story from the one she could ever have imagined,” she writes. “Through love, loss and the unexpected turns of life, she became part of a country that was once so distant from her own.”.

Industry observers note that in Dawn, public health specialist Muhammad Aftab Gohar argues the urgency of eliminating rabies in Pakistan. “The global goal is zero deaths from dog-transmitted rabies by 2030,” he writes. “A rabies-free Pakistan is within reach if we act together, and act now.”.

#7043. Latest Update: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

Latest Update: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
  • Industry observers note that at some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
  • In a recent development, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

Industry observers note that at some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

In a recent development, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

Recent findings suggest that yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

According to recent reports, in recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

At the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

According to recent reports, the success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

Industry observers note that international efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

Industry observers note that in the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

Industry observers note that today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

Worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

There is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

Recent findings suggest that A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France announced the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

Industry observers note that simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

Industry observers note that the integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

Together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will quickly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

In a recent development, political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

In this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

Industry observers note that but these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

Recent findings suggest that wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

According to recent reports, war also creates new dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

Finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to new waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

According to recent reports, the world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

But it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

Industry observers note that spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

From day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

Industry observers note that deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

Recent findings suggest that countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

Investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

Yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

Reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

Some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

Other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

The twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

All of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

Sources indicate that strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

The first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An enhancement to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly important, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The upcoming seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats presently occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

Permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

Another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral Latest START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

Yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

In a recent development, technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

The final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

It has been revealed that proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a latest UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

Recent findings suggest that halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

Ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

International financial institutions must be able to deliver financing rapidly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

This is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, introduced with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

It has been revealed that A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

  • So keen was the Philippines to have U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week from the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines: Trump stops by for 24 hours; Myanmar is still shut out despite junta lobbying; and Canada forges two latest trade deals in the region.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week from the ASEAN summit in Manila, Philippines: Trump stops by for 24 hours; Myanmar is still shut out despite junta lobbying; and Canada forges two newly introduced trade deals in the region.

So keen was the Philippines to have U.S. President Donald Trump attend the annual leader’s summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) that it changed the dates just for him. Originally scheduled to run five days earlier, it was shifted to run Nov. 15 through Nov. 17, the better to accommodate the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which is running yesterday and today in Shenzhen, China.

ASEAN can also take pleasure in the fact that Trump has now attended two years running. Under previous administrations, the nonattendance of the U.S. president or senior U.S. officials was a running complaint.

Sources indicate that after all the hoopla, then, what did the visit add up to? Not much, it seems.

Last year, when Kuala Lumpur hosted, the world was still gripped by questions about tariff negotiations. And Trump also got to play the peacemaker between Thailand and Cambodia—even though fighting between the two resumed the next month.

This time, no single issue defined the U.S. president’s visit, which lasted less than 24 hours. Trump proclaimed that the United States and Philippines had signed their biggest “ever” trade deal. But in typical Trump style, few details were forthcoming and nothing has actually been signed.

On a symbolic level for Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Trump’s arrival is a nice sign of the continued close relationship between the two countries.

It has been revealed that manila’s previous president, Rodrigo Duterte, was deeply skeptical of the United States, flirting with ending the two countries’ alliance in favor of a deal with China. Marcos has spun the other way, doubling down on the security relationship with Washington to push back against Beijing.

A few other deliverables were also duly delivered upon.

Industry observers note that A set of deals involving anti-scam initiatives was finalized. A “trade deal” with Thailand—which, like the Philippines deal, was not actually a final agreement—was announced.

Industry observers note that the leaders of the other Quad countries—Australia, Japan, and India—got a grand total of 55 scheduled minutes with Trump. The announcements that came out of that mainly repackaged old agreements.

And Marcos arranged for some food from Jollibee—the Philippines’ top fast-food chain and a national icon—to be delivered to Trump in the interest of “providing extra energy for all the work that you have to do.”.

At the state dinner, where Jollibee was not served, the U.S. president delivered a typically Trumpian speech. He assured ASEAN that he would support “partners and allies 100 percent,” adding that “when there’s a problem, you’ll call me.”.

He also took the opportunity to praise Marcos for his “very good genetics” as well as calling on Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto to stand up for compliments.

Industry observers note that some had expected announcements on Pax Silica, the United States’ global AI initiative. The United States is planning to build enormous semiconductor and data center facilities on land that used to house one of its military bases in the Philippines. But no announcements were forthcoming.

The Philippine government is keen on the idea as a way to boost its chips and electronics industry, as well as develop its defense industrial base. But the project is also controversial, spurring worries about the environmental impact and displacement of local people.

In a recent development, protesters took to the streets over Trump’s arrival to make their displeasure heard. Police reacted by blocking marches and detaining people. Nearly 300 demonstrators were arrested, according to protest organizers.

Don’t read too much into this, though. The Philippines is one of the few countries in the world where Trump is still popular. A poll by Pew Research Centre found that 68 percent of Filipinos trusted Trump to do the right thing, the highest of any country surveyed.

It has been revealed that overshadowing all of this was Trump’s next set of meetings in Shenzhen. Will he meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in a trilateral with Chinese President Xi Jinping? Maybe. Will he meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un? Also maybe.

So—at the end of the day—did Trump just stop by Manila for a pit stop, a photo op, and some Filipino fried food? Maybe.

It has been revealed that not yet… Myanmar isn’t back in ASEAN, yet. Despite determined lobbying from Thailand, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing still wasn’t invited to attend the ASEAN summit.

Industry observers note that since its 2021 coup, ASEAN has expressed its displeasure with Myanmar by not allowing junta leaders to attend summits. Senior civil servants get sent instead.

However, a leaders’ statement adopted on Sunday declared that ASEAN would pursue “calibrated engagement with Myanmar” and “may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation.”.

The widespread assumption is that come 2028, when Thailand is the chair of the bloc, the final barriers will be removed.

According to recent reports, the argument for reengagement is that, like it or not, the junta is there. Therefore, ASEAN countries need to engage—especially Thailand, which shares more than 2,000 kilometers of border with Myanmar.

In a recent development, critics will counter that engagement doesn’t seem to yield much. After the ASEAN summit, Min Aung Hlaing went on a rant in which he said that the statement on Myanmar was unreasonable. He also accused three unnamed member states of prejudice.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, in late October, fighting between junta forces and rebel groups on the Myanmar-Thia border saw explosives and shrapnel spill over to the Thai side. One Thai woman was wounded, and buildings were damaged.

Not quite… The draft “Code of Conduct on the South China Sea,” which the Philippines pushed so hard for, wasn’t finished. According to Marcos in his press conference at the end of the summit, it’s 85 percent done, and all that’s left is the defining of terms.

With the actual terms as yet unknown, there is, on the summit sidelines, a good deal of cynicism. Even if the agreement is finished next year, many see two decidedly nonthrilling options.

One is that in order for China to sign the agreement, it will have to be extremely thin, with little latest or binding terms in it. Second, if some reasonable guidelines are set out, China will just ignore them when it suits it.

Recent findings suggest that an analyst from a country with its own big claim on the waters suggested to me that a code of conduct could even be a disadvantage. If China breaks the rules, then other more rule-abiding countries might find their options to respond constrained by the agreement.

According to recent reports, not on the agenda… Remember the Thailand-Cambodia conflict? ASEAN doesn’t, it seems.

According to recent reports, following last summer’s fighting, ASEAN made an effort to address it. A Trump-sponsored peace deal was signed at the summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Following renewed fighting in December, an ASEAN observer team was confirmed. And in Cebu, Philippines, earlier this year, the two countries met on the sidelines for Philippine-brokered talks, even if the results were limited.

According to recent reports, this time around? Not a squeak. Partly to blame is perhaps that Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Manet didn’t attend. He was in Phnom Penh hosting the Francophonie Summit—see below.

Sorry for the secondhand smoke. During the ASEAN summit, Prabowo apologized to Malaysia and Singapore for how they have been affected by the haze from Indonesia’s vast forest fires last month.

He then rather undercut it by adding, “It is not our fault, but once again we apologize.”.

Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also proposed that ASEAN should establish a joint task force to probe companies linked to such fires. This would expand on the current bilateral Singapore-Indonesia task force established last month following some diplomatic spats on the topic.

Industry observers note that trade deals. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney dropped by on Saturday for the announcement that two trade deals were nearly done. Both an ASEAN-Canada and a Canada-Philippines trade deal have been forged with the aim of getting both signed next year.

Industry observers note that how much free trade will actually be in these agreements? It’s hard to tell with no text published, but past experience suggests that any changes will probably be more incremental than sweeping.

In a recent development, wow, everything’s computer. On Saturday, ASEAN signed its Digital Economy Framework Agreement, which should come into force in early 2027. The proclaimed aim is to create an “interconnected ASEAN digital marketplace.”.

Industry observers note that what does this mean in practice? The text’s not out yet, but this Singaporean government announcement lays out some broad strokes—mainly, accepting electronic trade documents, clearer rules on cross-border data flows, and a guarantee of no taxes on them for now, as well as cooperation on artificial intelligence and financial technology.

Oil stockpile. Indonesia, Japan, the Philippines, and Thailand agreed to set up shared stockpiles of diesel and gasoline to help manage future energy crises. The actual facilities will be built in Indonesia and Thailand.

Laos’s contestant, Thinla (center), performs during the grand final of the Eurovision Song Contest Asia 2026 at One Bangkok Forum in Bangkok on Nov. 14.Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP via Getty Images.

According to recent reports, cambodia: Cambodia hosted the Francophonie Summit from Saturday to Monday, gathering countries from across the French-speaking world—loosely defined. Prime Minister Hun Manet skipped ASEAN for this event and used it to do some diplomatic lobbying for Cambodia over its border dispute with Thailand, which infuriated the Thai government. French President Emmanuel Macron called for the investigation of the killing of a former opposition lawmaker and French Cambodian dual citizen Lim Kimya in Bangkok in 2025.

Sources indicate that indonesia: Police raided a data center owned by Megaspeed and found empty server racks. Prabowo is expected to pick a loyalist from his own party to be the next VP. Online phenomenon iShowSpeed highlighted off his Indonesian-speaking skills at an awards ceremony and then on a phone call with former U.S. President Barack Obama. And Nikkei has published a great article on Indonesia’s runners-for-hire who will burnish your Strava for you.

Recent findings suggest that malaysia: The governing coalition faced another setback with a loss in the Melaka state election. And Macron visited on Tuesday and pitched cooperation on rare earths, weapons, semiconductors, and nuclear energy to reduce dependence on the United States and China.

Joseph Rachman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly Southeast Asia Brief. He is a freelance journalist based in Bangkok. X: @rachman_joseph.

This includes the town council for Cork, Ireland, barring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from entering its city limits, citing his "illegal occupation of Palestine and bordering countries" and the continuous pro-Palestinian protests taking place every Saturday since October 2023, organized by the Cork Palestine Solidarity Campaign (CPSC).

Cork’s opposition to Israel adds context to the possible motives for why Daithí O’Corráin, an Irish national, allegedly destroyed a U.S. military C-130 Hercules aircraft in April. The incident also draws attention to several anti-Israel groups that have sprung up in Ireland in recent years.

IRELAND’S ELITES HAVE FOUND THEIR LATEST RELIGION: HATING ISRAEL.

Recent findings suggest that ireland’s anti-Israel foothold became international news in April when O’Corráin, a Cork native, barricaded himself inside a C-130, a U.S. military transport plane. Once inside, he tore out critical wiring, destroyed gauges, contaminated fuel tanks and even poured corrosive chemicals into the aircraft, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.

Although his motives remain unclear, several groups from Cork interpreted his actions as a form of resistance against Israel and U.S. military interventionism.

In one such case, a Cork business owner named Tracey Ryan debuted an initiative to raise €20,000 for O’Corráin's legal defense, praising his efforts to resist "the unwanted presence of U.S. military in Ireland in the face of their illegal war & support of Israel’s genocide.".

Sources indicate that "We, Daithí's friends and comrades, are raising funds to support him through his court case. We would really appreciate your support & will keep you updated here on ways to support Daithí," Ryan wrote in the description of the fundraising page.

In a recent development, according to her personal Facebook profile, Ryan joined a bus of pro-Palestinian activists who went to support O’Corráin at his court appearance. "Bus going to the high court to support Daithí on Thursday!!" Ryan wrote.

O’Corráin has also received support from CPSC, the Cork pro-Palestinian group.

As news of the incident spread, CPSC co-chair Anne McShane posted on her Palestinian advocacy Facebook page in support of O’Corráin, encouraging viewers to send him letters of encouragement after his incarceration.

Recent findings suggest that "Daithi needs our support in order to keep up his morale. Letters are a lifeline for prisoners," an April 17 post read.

CPSC spearheads anti-Israel demonstrations in Cork. In addition to hosting several pro-Palestinian fundraising initiatives, the group facilitates weekly Saturday demonstrations and invites speakers. At one point, CPSC’s website featured a fundraising site for O’Corráin, but the page has since been removed.

In CPSC’s own words, the group is part of a larger pro-Palestinian movement.

It has been revealed that "It’s not just the city. Towns across all of County Cork stand in solidarity with Palestinians, including Ballincollig, Bandon, Cobh, Charleville, Clonakilty, Fermoy, Kinsale, Macroom, Mallow, Mitchelstown, Skibbereen and more," the group states on its website.

"Cork Palestine Solidarity Campaign is a branch of the Irish Palestine Solidarity Campaign (IPSC)," it added.

As part of its sister groups’ efforts "to foster links between Palestine and Irish institutions and organizations," CPSC and IPSC have both applauded Cork’s city council efforts to promote pro-Palestinian policies.

"Well done to the Cork City Council which passed a motion … calling for the Central Bank to end the sale of Israeli bonds," one Facebook post reads.

For its own part, the Cork City Council has earned the support of IPSC and CPSC through a range of its official resolutions, making the town’s formal position to condemn any of Ireland’s ties to Israel.

In addition to banning Netanyahu from entering the city's limits in a 41-8 vote in 2024, Cork’s council has flown the Palestinian flag over city hall on U.N. International Day of Solidarity and called on Ireland to ban trade from Israeli settlements.

Cork has even passed a "twinning" mechanism with the Palestinian city of Nablus — a largely symbolic partnership.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Former Southern Poverty Law Center executive Heidi Beirich faces federal charges of wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy.
  • A former Southern Poverty Law Center official who led its hate-group tracking work told FBI agents he tried to make the watchdog’s controversial "Hate Map" more ideologically balanced, while saying Christians and conservatives were the first staffers pushed out in what he called a "long-term coup" at the organization after he left in 2013.
  • The former director mentioned he pushed for a more evenhanded SPLC, arguing that its "Hate Map" — which lists conservative groups alongside Ku Klux Klan chapters — should also include left-wing extremists, including violent animal-rights and extremist environmental groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Former Southern Poverty Law Center executive Heidi Beirich faces federal charges of wire fraud and money laundering conspiracy. The Department of Justice alleges Beirich hid over $4 million in payments from SPLC donors to fund White supremacy.

A former Southern Poverty Law Center official who led its hate-group tracking work told FBI agents he tried to make the watchdog’s controversial "Hate Map" more ideologically balanced, while saying Christians and conservatives were the first staffers pushed out in what he called a "long-term coup" at the organization after he left in 2013.

The former director mentioned he pushed for a more evenhanded SPLC, arguing that its "Hate Map" — which lists conservative groups alongside Ku Klux Klan chapters — should also include left-wing extremists, including violent animal-rights and extremist environmental groups. However, the former director said the effort met resistance and that, as liberal leaders reshaped the organization, most of his 17-person team was replaced.

"There was some kind of coup, long-term coup going on there between some, what I would — what I heard were some pretty liberal people, extreme people that had other ideas about what we were doing," the unnamed former director told agents, as first reported by The Daily Signal's Tyler O'Neil, who has been covering the SPLC's legal troubles.

DOJ EXPANDS INDICTMENT AGAINST SPLC, ALLEGING $4M SECRETLY FUNNELED TO KKK AND EXTREMIST GROUPS.

SPLC Intelligence Project Director Heidi Beirich speaks during an event on Jan. 12, 2018. (David Buchan/Variety/Penske Media via Getty Images).

According to recent reports, the former director’s comments appeared in an FBI interview transcript filed as an exhibit to Dr. Heidi Beirich’s Nov. 2 court filing. Beirich, a former SPLC official charged alongside the organization in a federal case alleging a scheme to mislead donors and banks about donations used to pay informants associated with violent extremist groups, pointed to multiple FBI interviews with an unnamed former SPLC director, identified in the filing as "Individual-1.".

In a January interview, Individual-1 told investigators he ran the SPLC’s field-source program, set up accounts used to pay sources and directed payments, according to Beirich’s filing. During a March 23 follow-up interview with Individual-1, FBI Special Agents David McDaniel and Parker Still framed the conversation around the program having "gone off the rails" under Beirich and told the former director they were not there to discuss the bank activity, noting he had "obviously nothing to do with all that," before questioning him about the SPLC’s alleged targeting of conservative organizations and Beirich’s role, according to the transcript.

EXCLUSIVE: SPLC'S 'FAR-LEFT,' 'ANTI-RACISM' CURRICULUM FOUND IN CLASSROOMS AS EARLY AS KINDERGARTEN: 'WATCHDOG'.

Individual-1 responded that, as his "gut impression," he believed her actions were political and accused some liberals at the center of having "a good degree of hatred" for conservatism, according to the March 23 transcript.

Individual-1 also alleged a shift in power at the SPLC. After he left in 2013, he noted, people were appointed to the SPLC’s board as "figureheads" and eventually gained enough voting power to take over the center. He said only one or two data-entry members of his roughly 17-person team remained, with the others replaced by staff he believed shared the new leadership’s politics.

Sources indicate that "That's who they ran off first were the Christians and conservatives," the unnamed former director told agents when asked why Beirich took the actions she did after his departure. "Then they — then the rest they just replaced with people they liked, you know, that agreed with them politically.".

HOW MUTINY AT SOUTHERN POVERTY LAW CENTER TRIGGERED LEADERSHIP COLLAPSE.

In a recent development, the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) building seen in March 2020 in Montgomery, Alabama. (Barry Lewis/InPictures via Getty Images).

In separate comments about the SPLC's controversial "Hate Map," Individual-1 stated he persuaded SPLC staff, despite internal resistance, to list Black separatist groups, which he considered comparable to White racist groups, on the map. However, he said he unsuccessfully pushed the SPLC to include violent animal-rights and environmental extremist groups and described his team’s approach during his tenure as director as "very nonpartisan" and "middle of the road.".

"We were very nonpartisan, or at least when I was running things, when I was director, we stayed right in the middle of the road," he stated.

In a June follow-up, the unnamed former director also criticized the SPLC's "Hate Map" for listing local chapters separately, saying it made the map's totals of the extremist groups it chose to identify look larger.

WATCH: SPLC CHIEF DOUBLES DOWN ON PLACING CHARLIE KIRK'S TURNING POINT USA ON 'HATE MAP'.

Sources indicate that while the unnamed former director was not charged in the SPLC case, Beirich was. Her lawyers say the interviews with the unnamed director warrant discovery into whether she was singled out because of her perceived role in the SPLC’s political speech, arguing that investigators’ questions about the SPLC’s treatment of conservative groups — and her alleged role in that work — could show the prosecution was motivated by hostility to the center’s political speech.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP.

"Individual-1’s statements confirm my longstanding criticism of the Southern Poverty Law Center, that it exaggerates ‘hate’ by inflating the chapters on its ‘hate map’ and that it systematically demonizes conservatives and Christians while turning a blind eye to extremism on the Left," O’Neil, the author of "Making Hate Pay: The Corruption of the Southern Poverty Law Center," told Fox News Digital. "Now, we have the former director of the Intelligence Project saying the SPLC appears to have pushed out Christians and conservatives, while rejecting his suggestion to include environmentalist agitators on the map.".

Fox News Digital reached out to the SPLC and attorneys for Heidi Beirich for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

These rules mark the most serious effort to close the loopholes that have allowed Chinese companies to obtain access to U.S. chips and computing power. It has been revealed that in the wake of Jensen Huang’s stunning resignation as CEO of Nvidia over his alleged affair with a Chinese spy, the U.S. Commerce Department this week revealed newly introduced export controls on artificial intelligence and semiconductors. These rules mark the most serious effort to close the loopholes that have allowed Chinese companies to obtain access to U.S. chips and computing power. The new interim rules target three vulnerabilities: Chinese rerouting of U.S.-made AI chips through third countries, rented access to AI computing power, and Chinese chip designers’ ability to manufacture advanced chips at non-Chinese facilities.

Sources indicate that the Nvidia scandal—including the alleged rerouting of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to China and the Trump administration’s apparent quiescence—underscores the scope of the Chinese threat to U.S. artificial intelligence technology. The new rules close vital gaps, but they do not resolve the threat. The next area where the United States is especially exposed is the Gulf, where the most advanced U.S. chips are now arriving, to be utilized in data centers operated by partners that maintain extensive ties with China.

According to recent reports, the Gulf magnifies the Nvidia problem. Both the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are trying to shift their economies away from oil, and they’re placing AI at the center of their strategies. In May 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump declared that both countries would be able to purchase advanced U.S. chips to help facilitate these efforts. Abu Dhabi and Riyadh are financing massive AI buildouts, where Nvidia chips will be installed, operated, and even rented to customers or cloud tenants. The two monarchies are taking advantage of their desert land areas, access to lower-cost energy, and deep coffers, offering Nvidia an appealing market and affording Washington an opportunity to keep U.S. technology at the center of the AI buildout.

Recent findings suggest that both the Saudis and the Emiratis, however, also maintain deep relations with China. Washington fears that Beijing could gain access, intentional or not, through its contractors or cloud customers—or via hardware or software that may be connected to U.S. systems or chips. Chinese infiltration could occur through a trusted partner, with or without their knowledge, without directly acquiring the restricted chips.

Sources indicate that that’s why companies such as the UAE’s Group 42 have caught the eye of China watchers and technology hawks. The group’s past links to China and its tech sector, even though the manufacturer publicly renounced them after the Biden administration declared it a security risk, raise questions that diplomatic assurances cannot resolve. The issue is not what the company states but whether its operations, ownership, partnerships, and access to sensitive technology can be independently verified and insulated from possible Chinese exploitation.

According to recent reports, saudi Arabia presents a similar challenge. The kingdom is pursuing AI autonomy by seeking control over every layer of the technology stack. But Washington will want evidence that Saudi officials can protect their data centers and cloud services from unauthorized access. And that case is increasingly difficult to make as Saudi Arabia continues to partner with both U.S. and Chinese technology companies.

The new rules make the Gulf an notable litmus test for whether Washington can enforce its new approach in third-country data centers. Gulf-based facilities will need to prevent restricted people from accessing compute power enabled by U.S. chips, including indirectly through the cloud or other intermediaries. It’s not just about whether a Chinese company or user can rent compute power through a Gulf partner, but also whether the safeguards are in place for partners who maintain U.S. compute power to verify ownership and the affiliations of users.

It has been revealed that U.S. export controls were designed for trade in tangible goods, but the Commerce Department has now acknowledged that simply controlling the physical movement of chips is not enough. The newly introduced rules extend export controls to some forms of remote access and computing power—intended, for example, to prevent a Chinese tech giant from renting access to a processor through a data center or cloud provider. The new rule is a major step forward but not a complete solution. Safeguarding U.S. chips will require more than protecting the physical product or regulating direct access. It will require oversight of the people and systems that can use the computing power that those chips provide. That means guarding not just the chips’ physical location but also their ownership, network architecture, and consumer access.

Instead of determining which country or firm is purchasing a chip, an export policy will need to ask who will own and operate the facility, who can administer the compute power, which customers can rent its processors, what the networking and software infrastructure is made of, the nationality of consumers, and even whether the systems can be accessed outside of where they are housed. A processor being utilized in a Gulf data center, for example, may be used to provide computing power to a restricted Chinese tech giant or state institution through the cloud—so controls must follow the user, not just the export.

Nvidia sells the most advanced chips in the business. Its former CEO, who made himself the face of the tech giant’s strategy and government relations, was close with Trump and has decried more stringent export controls on AI chips, arguing that such restrictions will merely move more consumers toward Chinese suppliers like Huawei. His influence may have helped persuade Trump to sell limited amounts of the H200 chip to China. But the concern extends beyond Huang’s influence. Questions about the administration’s handling of the policy—including conflicts of interest involving U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Trump’s own financial interests in Nvidia, and other relationships between U.S. officials and companies that may have benefited from certain sales, like Jared Kushner’s—warrant a review of these decisions. Regulators should begin by reexamining the decision to allow the sale of Nvidia’s most advanced chips to Saudi Arabia and the UAE.

In a recent development, A new oversight policy would not entail a crackdown on Nvidia or a blanket ban on selling further advanced chips to Gulf states. Instead, Washington would expand access only when Gulf states meet specific conditions and establish guidelines for continuously evaluating who can access the technology. The new framework should become the baseline for future Gulf licenses that can identify approved facilities and consumers; limit chip quantities and aggregate compute power; prohibit restricted access and rentals; and require oversight of inventories, access logs, and control standards. Washington should also retain the right to suspend a license at any time. China has already sought to lease capacity through data centers in Europe and accessed U.S. chips to train its models through systems in Thailand.

It has been revealed that when the Democrats take control of the U.S. Congress in January, they will likely press for tougher oversight of foreign chip deals—as they should. Democrats and Republicans have a considerable opportunity to work together on this concern. Even though this week’s new rules help address some of the areas of concern, they are an executive branch policy and thus subject to change at any moment. Congress can focus on passing the Remote Access Security Act, which will require export policy to include remote access controls, and the AI Overwatch Act, which will give Congress more oversight over foreign chip sales.

Sources indicate that for the UAE and Saudi Arabia, access to the most advanced chips is still possible but now comes with stronger U.S. demands—and any failure to adhere to those conditions should mean that access is immediately cut off. Fair or not, the Nvidia scandal raises the cost of assuming that trust is enough protection.

In a recent development, however, tighter U.S. restrictions also carry some risk. If U.S. requirements become too stringent, intrusive, costly, or unpredictable, Gulf governments may turn back toward Chinese tech or tilt toward other suppliers with fewer restrictions. Greater reliance on Chinese tech would not replace the U.S. technological edge overnight but over the long term, it could well reduce U.S. influence.

Sources indicate that the UAE and Saudi Arabia are seeking slightly different things. The UAE is leading the space in dealmaking and pushing the next generation of AI models, while Saudi Arabia is seeking to build out local compute capacity. For both, ongoing relationships with Chinese tech companies will remain an glitch, and Washington will need stringent controls and verifications on who can access and use the systems.

China’s challenge to U.S. AI is a serious threat, and the United States must strengthen its technological defenses in the Gulf and elsewhere. The Commerce Department’s latest rules are a meaningful step in closing the regulatory gap in U.S. export policy on chips. The Saudis’ and Emiratis’ AI ambitions make them key tests of whether the United States can enforce this approach. That requires systematic and continuous scrutiny of many more layers of the AI value chain than current U.S. export controls offer, including ownership, users, infrastructure, and remote access. The Saudis and Emiratis will, of course, say that they can be trusted. But in the post-Huang AI space, it is simply too risky to rely on assurances alone.
